A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CrossIC-PT. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching content across table consolidation, renumbering, and expanded appendices.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendix B report original continued-pretraining experiments across three models and six languages, including ablations and English-retention evaluations.

after.justification: The original empirical evaluations remain, supplemented by new controls, Chinese and Vietnamese results, and instruction-tuned-model and extended-context experiments.

M1.justification: The bilingual article construction, paragraph segmentation, English-first concatenation, [SPLIT]-based sliding windows, next-word prediction, LoRA training, and retrieval procedure remain unchanged. Newly disclosed implementation choices and additional experimental configurations do not establish a revised method.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds Chinese and Vietnamese evaluations using Llama-3.1-8B on the existing seven task types. This extends language coverage beyond the original six languages; the training sources and task families remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Section 4.4 and Table 2 add X-MONO-PT, which trains on target-language data alone, and remove the Llama-2-7B/EMMA-500 comparison. LEIA and Mix-PT remain. The Qwen appendix labels Cross-CPT and CrossIC-CPT match the retained methods rather than establishing additional comparators.

E3.justification: The evaluation design expands with retrieved-data-only training and randomized bilingual-pair controls, a Thai instruction-tuned Llama experiment with learning rate 5e-6, and a Thai Qwen2.5-1.5B comparison of 4096- versus 8192-token windows. Original training and prompting settings remain. Appendix D inconsistently identifies its model as Llama-3 in prose and Llama-3.1 in Table 8.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained sliding-window, concatenation-direction, checkpoint, and English-retention analyses, v2 adds a direct random-pair ablation of semantic relatedness, a retrieved-data-only comparison, instruction-tuned-model limitations analysis, and context-length sensitivity testing. These substantially broaden validation of the method's components and applicability.

E5.justification: Both versions report LEIA using seeds 32, 111, and 222 with means and variability, and retain the same English-performance significance reporting in Figure 6. Additional detailed LEIA rows use the existing reporting practice; no new uncertainty-estimation procedure is established.

E6.justification: Expanded Appendix B supplies language-by-task results, while new controls and Appendices C–E add substantial outcomes. Table 7 reports CrossIC-PT averages of 46.08 for Chinese and 47.02 for Vietnamese; Table 9 reports 42.23 at 4096 tokens versus 43.56 at 8192 tokens. Most original headline scores remain, while EMMA-500 results disappear. Some new appendix entries conflict with retained main-table values.

T1.justification: The mathematical article and paragraph constructions in Section 3.2 are unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive mathematical derivation or assumption.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about non-parallel semantic pairing, window construction, and retrieval augmentation. The headline improvements of 3.79%, 3.99%, and 1.95% also remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly qualifies effectiveness on instruction-tuned models and suggests a mismatch between fine-tuning and pre-training objectives as an explanation. The original Limitations section remains unchanged, including its 4096-token-only restriction, which now conflicts with Appendix E.

D1.justification: V2 identifies the gte-multilingual-base retrieval encoder, the 20240720 Wikipedia dumps, and wikiextractor processing. Appendix A adds the SacreBLEU configuration and Japanese/Korean/Thai pre-tokenization code. These clarify previously undisclosed implementation choices without establishing changes to the original experiments.

R1.justification: The bibliography contains the same works, and Section 2 retains the same positioning against parallel-corpus and code-switching approaches. An added unresolved citation marker does not identify a new cited work or establish revised research positioning.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites of the method introduction, baseline descriptions, ablation discussion, and analysis opening, alongside expanded appendices. V2 also adds Fei Huang and expands acknowledgements. Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: V1's Tables 2–3 are consolidated into an expanded Table 2 with data-source groups and an average column. The appendix task-average table is replaced by detailed language-specific tables, and Tables 7–9 display new experiments. Figure 5 gains a random-pair series, revised legend, and changed vertical range; other main figures remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added semantic-pairing control and monolingual baseline strengthen validation, while implementation details improve reproducibility and instruction-tuned tests expose an applicability boundary. These gains are tempered by inconsistencies: Portuguese W+F CrossIC-PT scores are 49.97 in Table 2 but 49.51 in Table 6, and the retained 4096-token limitation contradicts Appendix E. Overall, evidence and transparency improve, with unresolved reporting problems limiting the gain.
